title: House Bill Would Lift H-1B Salary Exemption Threshold Toward $140,000
excerpt: Rep. Glenn Grothman's bill, matching Sen. Jon Husted's Senate version, would replace the $60,000 threshold frozen since 1998 with twice the National Average Wage Index — nearly $140,000 today — for H-1B-dependent employers using the salary exemption.
body:
• A House bill introduced October 13 by Rep. Glenn Grothman, with a Senate companion from Sen. Jon Husted, would replace the $60,000 H-1B salary exemption threshold, unchanged since 1998, with a formula set at twice the Social Security Administration's National Average Wage Index.
  • At the current index of nearly $70,000, the new threshold would be nearly $140,000, and it would rise automatically as U.S. wages grow.
  • The change targets only the salary route: H-1B-dependent employers could still use the existing exemption for workers holding a master's degree or higher.
  • For Indian professionals at H-1B-dependent firms: if the bill passes, a salary below the new threshold would no longer exempt your employer from first recruiting U.S. workers and meeting displacement attestations before sponsoring you.

Rep. Glenn Grothman of Wisconsin introduced the Protecting American Workers Through H-1B Modernization Act in the House on October 13, according to VisaVerge, completing a two-chamber push that began when Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio filed the Senate version on October 7, IANS reported. The bill would scrap the fixed $60,000 salary threshold that has governed a key H-1B employer exemption since 1998 and replace it with a wage-linked formula.

How the exemption works today

Under current law, employers classified as H-1B-dependent — companies where H-1B workers make up a specified share of the workforce — must meet added obligations before hiring more H-1B staff. They generally have to attest that they recruited U.S. workers in good faith and that they have not displaced U.S. workers, including in some placements at another employer's worksite. An employer can avoid those added requirements for a given worker in two ways: pay the worker at least $60,000 a year, or hire a worker who holds a master's degree or higher in a field related to the job. The bill rewrites only the first test. The degree route would stay exactly as it is.

Why $140,000, and why a formula

The $60,000 figure was not arbitrary when Congress set it in 1998. According to Husted's office, it represented twice the Social Security Administration's National Average Wage Index at the time. Congress never built in an adjustment, so the number sat frozen for 28 years while wages rose around it. The sponsors' material puts the index now at nearly $70,000, which makes twice the index nearly $140,000. Rather than pick a new fixed number that would age the same way, the bill ties the threshold to the index itself, so it moves as U.S. wages move. Readers can see how H-1B status and extensions work in practice on the USCIS H-1B guidance page.

"That's not modernization, that's a loophole."

— Sen. Jon Husted, on the $60,000 threshold unchanged since 1998

Husted argued that companies heavily reliant on H-1B visas should not be able to use an outdated salary figure to avoid offering jobs to qualified American workers first. Grothman made the same case from the House side, saying American workers should come first and that there was no excuse for leaving the threshold unchanged for so long. Full details of both bills and the sponsors' statements are in VisaVerge's coverage of the Grothman bill.

What it would mean for Indian professionals

Indian nationals are the largest single national group among H-1B holders, and many work for the large technology and IT-services firms most likely to be classed as H-1B-dependent. The practical effect would fall on mid-level roles paid between $60,000 and the new threshold. A worker in that band would no longer qualify the employer for the salary exemption, so the employer would have to complete the recruitment and non-displacement attestations for that hire — or rely on the worker's advanced degree, where one exists. Senior roles already paid above the new level would be unaffected, and employers that are not H-1B-dependent are outside this provision entirely.

Separate from the $100,000 fee and the wage-weighted lottery

The bill addresses a different part of the system from the two other big 2026 H-1B changes. A presidential proclamation in September added a $100,000 payment requirement for certain H-1B petitions, and the Department of Homeland Security has replaced the random cap lottery with a wage-level-weighted selection system. Those measures govern entry and selection. This bill governs employer obligations after a company is already hiring at scale through the program.

What happens next

The measure is not law. It must pass both the House and the Senate and be signed by the president before any threshold changes, and until then the $60,000 salary exemption and the master's-degree exemption both remain in force. No committee vote had been reported as of publication. Employers and workers planning 2027 filings should track the bill's progress in Congress rather than change current petitions, which continue under existing rules.
